paper_title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Chollet (2019) argued that intelligence should be measured by how efficiently system turns priors and experience into skill, on tasks that lie largely outside its experience and have verifiable answer. ARC is the concrete instance of that argument, and on its current edition the gap between what person solves in minute and what model solves from the same demonstrations is still significant (Chollet et al., 2026). For agent systems that continually operate for days and weeks, more pressing question is whether skill acquired on one job is still there the next time similar scenario is met, which we call memorization, and whether that experience makes the system better at similar jobs it has never met, which we call generalization. By design, ARC measures acquisition once, within single episode, and does not ask either over longer horizons. The benchmarks that do ask it have three limitations (Section 5). Firstly, each is built around one applied domain, such as coding or office work (Wu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2025), in which the models under test already know great deal from the pretraining data, and gains may come partly from drawing out that knowledge. Secondly, most serve fixed set of instances, each seen once, so the same conceptual task never returns with fresh input. This means memorized answer cannot be told apart from more abstract learned skill. Finally, while some permit both (Wu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025), most assume single family of learner, gradient updates for fine-tuning suites such as MLLM-CTBench (Guo et al., 2025) and prompting and memory for agent benchmarks such as AgentCL and PATH-Bench (Shu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). 1 Preprint. Under review. We propose Continual-ARC, lifelong stream built from ARC, where tasks need no knowledge of any domain beyond core-knowledge priors, such as objectness and counting (Chollet, 2019), and the rule of each task has to be induced from few demonstrations. The models we test solve some of these tasks at first sight, but far from all (Appendix K). Continual-ARC has track for each of ARCs three editions, which rise in difficulty (Chollet et al., 2025; ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a), to the point where cheaper models and frontier models are best measured on different tracks. For our ARC-AGI-1 track, the Re-ARC generators (Hodel, 2024) produce fresh, verified instance of any ARC-AGI-1 training task on demand. task then returns after dormant gap as often as the stream asks, each time with new input that no cached answer fits. New tasks also keep arriving throughout the stream. On each instance, the system may submit an answer and receive bare verdict (paying for incorrect attempts), pay for demonstration, or take actions inside the harness if one is provided. We score the instance by the share of this feedback budget it used, all of it if the instance fails, as Chollet (2019) proposed for an interactive version of ARC. After the stream, we freeze the system and test it on fresh instances of the streams tasks, which measures memorization, and on 100 tasks from ARC-AGI-1s evaluation set that the stream never shows, which measures generalization. Because system may carry anything between instances, prompting, memory and weight updates all face the same stream and the same tests. Most of our experiments focus on one agent harness, prime-agent (Karten et al., 2026), on Qwen3.59B and GLM-5.3 Flash. We compare it with two prompting floors and program-induction method, and with the weights of student, Qwen3.5-9B, trained to imitate teacher, GLM-5.3 Flash (Ross et al., 2011). In some runs GLM-5.3 Flash also writes Qwen3.5-9Bs notes, so that notes and weights are taught by the same teacher. On returning tasks, we find that the harness saves less than floor that simply caches each tasks demonstrations, with either model, and only the teachers harness keeps up with the program-induction method, when explicitly told to store one program per task (Figure 3 and Section 4). On unseen tasks, notes and programs save nothing measurable, while training on the teachers moves makes the student considerably better. We also define collective regimes in which one system serves 2 or 4 users at once, each operating on non-overlapping tasks of their own (Section 2.5). This simulates working environment in which people are responsible for different tasks and the learning is collective over the group. More concurrent users generate more varied training data over the streams 200 rounds, and our results show that this leads to better generalization to unseen tasks. In contrast, no harness-based method gains on the unseen tasks whatsoever. Our benchmark highlights significant shortcomings in how much off-the-shelf harnesses can learn in unfamiliar domains, and opens the door to research on training models to drive harnesses in such domains.

sections.title: 2.3 TWO TESTS AFTER THE STREAM
sections.content: The stream measures what learner keeps while it learns. To measure what it has at the end, we freeze the learner and serve it two tests, each single round of 100 instances. The learner is not told that test has begun. We start every test instance from the learners state at the end of the stream, and nothing learned on one test instance reaches another. The seen test consists of four fresh instances of each of the streams 25 tasks, at instance seeds the stream did not use, and measures memorization. In the held-out test, which measures generalization, 100 evaluation tasks never seen on the stream are served once each. learner that keeps one program per task gets cheaper on the seen test but no cheaper on the held-out test, whereas learner that has become better solver of new tasks gets cheaper on both. Plotting the two tests against each other (Figure 3) is the continual counterpart of plotting in-distribution against out-of-distribution accuracy (Miller et al., 2021). 2.4 MEASURING LEARNING over the stream mixes what learner could already do before the stream with what it learns along the way. To measure the learning alone, we need one more run, the reset: the same learner on the same stream and the same tests, with its state wiped before each instance. sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: We report results on ARC-AGI-1 here, with early results for ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3 in Appendix K. Table 1 gives the share learned on the stream, L, and the share saved on the two tests, Sseen and Sheld, for GLM-5.3 Flash (G) and Qwen3.5-9B (Q). Figure 3 plots absolute and relative solve rates, and budget used and share saved, Sseen and Sheld. Figure 4 plots each methods share solved and budget by task visit. We also test GPT-6 Luna at high effort in prime-agent (Karten et al., 2026), hermes-agent (Nous Research, 2026) and openclaw (OpenClaw contributors, 2026), see Figure 5. Shares saved below are read at the lower right quadrants of Figures 3 and 5. Baselines. Against the stateless floors (QC0, GC0), the demo-cache floors (QC, GC) saved Sseen = 0.37 [0.26, 0.51] and 0.44 [0.34, 0.57] respectively (Figure 3), which is the saving from not paying for the demonstrations twice. On new tasks there was nothing to replay, so the saving was nil, with Sheld = 0.01 and 0.02. The program libraries (QP, GP) beat the demo caches by wide margin on the seen test, with Sseen = 0.65 [0.46, 0.86] and 0.81 [0.59, 1.00] respectively (Appendix F), but they also saved nothing measurable in Sheld, with 0.03 [0.02, 0.09] and 0.05 [0.06, 0.14]. This is to be expected, as program verified on the demonstrations of one task does not solve another. Harnesses as shipped. Left to their own prompting, only saved measurably on either test across three harnesses, four models, and GPT-6 Lunas three efforts (Figures 3 to 5 and Appendix K). This was despite the instructions at the start of every session stating that tasks recur with fresh inputs, that each instance starts new conversation, and that each demonstration or incorrect attempt costs one (Appendix C). Neither harness (Q, G) beat its demo-cache floor (QC, GC; Figure 3). Further, neither expert guidance (QE) nor asking the harness to save liberally (QA, Appendix F) saved measurably, nor did the teachers notes (QT and QTE), despite the teacher leaving 106 and 104 notes and files, respectively. For all of these, Sseen lies between 0.01 and 0.06, and Sheld between 0.02 and 0.03. Even G, which solved nearly every instance, still spent 13.6% of the budget per solved instance after every task had been met, against 17.5% for G0 (Figure 4, right), where perfect memory spends nothing. We investigated this: kept rule in words for every task in prime-agents store, but the harness only showed six entries per instance, chosen before the task was known, so the rule reached on only 40 of 154 returns (Appendix E.2). To investigate further, we also read what each of the three harnesses (H) stored with GPT-6 Luna driving (Figure 5 and Appendix E). prime-agent kept an entry for later sessions only when the agent saved it as global, as its prompt explained, and the agent never did. hermes-agent loaded its skills on every return, but they held general advice which did not affect spend. openclaw never promoted memory at all, and an earlier correct answer never came back on any of its returns. None of the three harnesses kept the demonstrations it paid for, each buying 2.3 to 3.9 pairs per instance where the demo-cache floor bought 1.4 to 2.6. This suggests that the harnesses own prompting is not well suited to this domain. 8 Preprint. Under review. Asking to store. Given that several harnesses were failing to store anything, we tried explicitly prompting the harnesses after every verdict to save very liberally anything that could help with the tasks future instances (H-A). However, this only made measurable difference for prime-agent on the seen test. With GPT-6 Luna driving, it saved Sseen = 0.42 [0.29, 0.55], while hermes-agents 0.18 [0.01, 0.39] and openclaws 0.07 [0.02, 0.17] were within noise of nothing (Figure 5). With GLM driving, it saved 0.26 [0.13, 0.39] (GA), and with Qwen it was also within noise, at 0.02 [0.02, 0.07] (QA). Overall, the harnesses still gained little from persistence, despite the prompting. Expert guidance. To see if we could push the performance of the harnesses further, we added expert guidance, which explicitly told the harness to write Python programs to solve the tasks, verify each program against the demonstrations, save it for its task and reuse it. With it, GE saved Sseen = 0.74 [0.64, 0.84] and the three harnesses on GPT-6 Luna (H-E) saved 0.62 to 0.72 (Figure 5). memorized only when the teacher wrote its notes and both were given the guidance (QETE), with Sseen = 0.34 [0.26, 0.42]. This shows that the harnesses were fully capable of performing well, and that the failure was combined lack of judgment of the model and failure of the harness prompts to encourage the correct behavior in this domain. Generalization. The Re-ARC generators derive all 400 ARC-AGI-1 training rules from one library of 160 primitive functions (Hodel, 2024), and therefore the seen and held-out tasks both share the same building blocks. harness which learns to abstract and store these shared building blocks during the stream could then theoretically use these to improve performance on the held-out tasks. Despite this, none of the harness methods generalized measurably (Table 1, Figure 5 and Appendix A). This includes QETE, in which GLM, given the expert guidance, played the whole stream and wrote every program and note, solving 98% of the instances, which Qwen failed to put to use on the held-out test. In contrast, training the weights generalized measurably, with DAgger (QDE) saving Sheld = 0.29 [0.23, 0.35], half its Sseen = 0.57 [0.48, 0.67]. Untrained, Qwen actually struggled to use the harness at all, solving only 18 of the 100 held-out tasks in prime-agent (Q0) against 31 in the stateless loop (QC0). As result, part of what DAgger learned was simply to drive the harness. This quirk is visible in Figure 3 (top left), where the harness method resets sit below those of QC and QP. Providing expert guidance to the untrained Qwen in the harness offsets some of this degradation, lifting its held-out solves from 1326 to 2233 per play (Appendix H). DAgger, however, solved 47 to 52, beyond both, and so also learned something fundamental about ARC itself, on top of learning to drive the harness and distilling the expert guidance. More users. At two and four users (QDE(2) and QDE(4)), each bringing 25 tasks of their own, DAggers adapter trained on the games of 50 and 100 tasks. On the held-out test it then saved Sheld = 0.40 at two users and 0.39 at four (Figure 3). Seemingly, DAgger reached diminishing returns for generalization beyond two users. The full training dynamics are shown in Appendix H.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: We screened roughly two hundred benchmarks and methods. Table 8 (Appendix G) sets the closest against the five properties that this benchmark combines: fresh instance on every exposure, recurrence after variable gaps, task set that grows through the stream, binary feedback that is charged, and protocol open to prompting, memory and weight updates. We found no work that has all five. ARC. Chollet (2019) notes that ARCs format is close-ended, weakness that motivates this work, and suggests that better one would let the test-taker query an example generator and submit answers for feedback repeatedly, with the feedback consumed as the score. To our knowledge, this has not been implemented, although Re-ARC (Hodel, 2024) supplies the generators and verifiers it needs. The strongest ARC-AGI-1 systems instead adapt their weights at test time and discard the adaptation, per task (Akyürek et al., 2024; Franzen et al., 2025) or over the evaluation set (Pourcel et al., 2025), never meeting fresh instance of task they have adapted to. ArcMemo (Ho et al., 2025) writes concepts to memory, but over single fixed pass. Over stream of generated ARCstyle tasks, Zhang et al. (2026a) find that memory the model keeps rewriting first helps and then degrades. ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a) moves to learning over time within single game, and harness that keeps per-game notes across runs (Bedi, 2026) has saturated its public games, untested on others. 9 Preprint. Under review. Continual learning. The classic protocol (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017; van de Ven & Tolias, 2019) is fixed sequence of tasks with free labels, scored on fixed test sets after each task boundary. Where tasks come back at all, they return as planned second pass (Wołczyk et al., 2021; Powers et al., 2022; Veniat et al., 2021) or as unannounced revisits (Caccia et al., 2020; Hemati et al., 2023). Fresh instances are standard in reinforcement learning environments (Cobbe et al., 2020; Küttler et al., 2020) and in generated reasoning suites with verifiers (Stojanovski et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026), but these suites train first and test afterwards, and supervision is free. Agent benchmarks. StreamBench (Wu et al., 2024) gives binary feedback in one shuffled pass, MemoryBench (Ai et al., 2025) feedback from simulated users, LifelongAgentBench (Zheng et al., 2025) brings skills back but not instances, and SWE-Bench-CL (Joshi et al., 2025) regroups SWEBench by repository. CL-Bench (Asawa et al., 2026) scores stateful system against stateless one, and AgentCL (Shu et al., 2026) and PATH-Bench (Yang et al., 2026) rerun stream or reinsert probe task. All draw from fixed pool of instances that appear once or recur unchanged. None grows the task set, charges for supervision or serves many users, and most evaluate prompting and memory only. Concurrent work (Anonymous, 2026c; Zheng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a) neither charges for feedback nor trains weights. Memory against weights. The comparison between memory and weights exists only in pieces. Memory-based agents (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Suzgun et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Nekoei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b) are motivated by the cost or forgetting of fine-tuning but seldom compare against it, and the closest to our program library keeps skill as program once it runs correctly (Wang et al., 2025). On-policy reinforcement learning is reported to forget less than supervised fine-tuning (Shenfeld et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a), but to forget severely over sequence of tasks (Luo et al., 2026), as does harness learning as tasks drift (Chen et al., 2026b). SEAL (Zweiger et al., 2025) runs self-directed weight updates on ARC, test-time curricula (Hübotter et al., 2025) train on tasks chosen for the target, and self-improving harnesses (Karten et al., 2026) rewrite their memory and skills, but each is evaluated on its own terms. Concurrently, Self-Direction (Kansal et al., 2026) distills an agents reflections into LoRA adapter, on task sets recurring at most three times. Memory and weights have yet to be compared on tasks that keep returning.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: To the best of our knowledge, Continual-ARC is the first benchmark to compare harness-based and weight-based learners under one score, in domain where both can memorize and generalize. We have shown that most harnesses as shipped did not learn measurably in this domain. How well they learn in other domains remains open. Simple expert guidance greatly improved how much they memorized (Figure 5), which shows that the default harness prompts were not sufficient to inform the models what to store, though more powerful models may fare better. Training the weights proved important in this domain, as DAgger learned from short stream of tasks to solve new ones where in-context learning through the harness did not. Continual-ARC targets the continual learning that one person or small team meets over short horizon, from 200 instances rather than post-training corpus. We are therefore most excited about weight-based algorithms that learn from sparse data, model-based reinforcement learning above all (Kaiser et al., 2020). The DAgger algorithm we used is relatively simple form of weight-based learning, as it needs stronger teacher whose reasoning tokens are available. Teacher-free reinforcement learning from the sparse reward (Shao et al., 2024), on-policy self-distillation (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026) and on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024) are natural next steps (Appendix reports our first attempts). Trust-region updates (Schulman et al., 2015) would also keep such learner from degrading what its users receive, which is essential in real deployments. One weakness of this study is that most of its runs used relatively small models on ARC-AGI-1, the easiest of our three tracks. We leave it to future work to test stronger models on the ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3 tracks (Appendix K). This will let us investigate how much guidance frontier models need in order to store what matters in harness, and how efficiently they learn it in their weights, both for memorization and generalization. In the long run, we expect the harness to become less the system itself and more the infrastructure that trains the inner model, continually distilling content into the weights and staying thin rather than accumulating an ever-growing list of files. 10 Preprint. sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used an AI coding assistant (Claude, Anthropic) throughout this work. It drafted the abstract and every section of this paper from the first authors notes, which record each design decision, the reason for it, the objection reviewer would raise, and the answer. The first author edited every draft, and then rewrote the main text line by line. It carried out the literature search behind Section 5 and Appendix G, screening roughly two hundred works. The first author checked every entry in the tables against the works own abstract, and every comparative claim in the paper against those notes. It proposed parts of the experimental grid of Section 3, and the first author decided on them. It wrote most of the code in the repositories that we release, including the ARC-AGI-2 and ARCAGI-3 environments, the harness adapters and DAggers training, under tests and smoke runs that the first author reviewed. It also launched and monitored the runs on remote machines at the first authors direction. Finally, it computed the analyses of Section 4 and Appendices and from the run records, including the paired comparisons and their intervals, and it read the harnesses stored state for Appendix E. Every table and figure is regenerated from the run directories when the paper is built. Scripts in the papers repository recompute the numbers quoted in Section 4 and the paired comparisons of Appendices and F. No AI was used to generate data. Every instance in the stream comes from the Re-ARC generators, ARC-GENs generators or our level generators for the ARC-AGI game engine. The rules of the private set are the exception (Appendix J). Six agents on Claude Opus 5.5, one for each family of rules, wrote the 98 candidates as generators and solvers in code, and models calibrated them, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, GLM-5.3 Flash and Qwen3.5-9B answering fresh instances at first sight. The filters, the screens and the selection that kept 50 of them are code written with the assistant, and no person has tried the rules. No AI was used to prove claims, and the equations in Section 2 are definitions. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work involves no human subjects and no personal data. Every public task of the benchmark comes from the public ARC-AGI tasks and games or from the Re-ARC and ARC-GEN generators, which the software fetches from their sources and does not redistribute. ARC-AGI-3 levels are charged against the human baselines that ARC Prize publishes. The rules of the private set are our own, and we do not release them (Appendix J). The harnesses we evaluate write and run their own code, and one reached the evaluation itself in an early run. Section 3 and Appendix describe how we confine each one, and we recommend the same to anyone running agents on the benchmark. Our findings are negative for three publicly available harnesses, none of them from the first authors employer, which builds agent systems. We run each as its authors ship it, with its persistence switched on, and we trace each shortfall to specific step in its design (Appendix E). Appendix gives each ones configuration and reports that prime-agents Python skills, refine among them, did not load in our runs. The adapters are released with the code, so that the harnesses authors can check how their systems were run. Continual learning in deployment also raises questions of privacy that this benchmark does not address. In the collective regime, one system learns from many users at once, and what it keeps from one user could reach another. Our streams are abstract puzzles with no user data, and the benchmark does not measure leakage between users.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Section 2 defines the streams and their measures, which the benchmark computes from runs records, the share learned from run and the resets, and Appendices A, and give every streams parameters and the process that generates each stream (Algorithm 1). Streams are deterministic, so every system meets the same instances in the same order. Appendix gives every text that learner is shown, or the file in the code that holds it, and Appendix describes how we run each harness, 11 Preprint. Under review. with the versions of every component. Appendix and Appendix give the model presets and the rule that chose them, and Appendix gives DAggers settings. Every adapter DAgger played with is kept, so any rounds student can be played again. The code of the benchmark and of every learner, including the harness adapters, is released with the records of every run this paper reports. The rules of the private set are withheld by design, since released rule could be learned before run, and Appendix gives how they were made and chosen. Each verified run is requested on the benchmark repositorys public issues, and its numbers are posted there. The models are sampled through provider APIs and on our own servers, so rerun will differ from ours by about the spread we report, such as how far chance moves S, which the learners that keep nothing between instances show (Section 4).

sections.title: A BENCHMARK DETAILS
sections.content: ARC-AGI-1. We draw the stream from the 400 ARC-AGI-1 training tasks through the Re-ARC generators (Hodel, 2024), pinned by commit. Given task id and seed, the generator produces an input grid and the verifier produces its output, and we keep only the pairs that the verifier accepts, discarding any demonstration whose input equals the test input. Each demonstration request draws one more such pair. learner cannot cache outputs, since every instance is fresh, and caching demonstrations has price. The held-out test draws on the 400 ARC-AGI-1 evaluation tasks, which have no generators, and each of them appears once, with its original demonstrations available on request. request returns them one at time, two to seven of them and three or four for most tasks of the track, and nothing after them. The held-out tasks are public. The held-out tests 100 tasks come from ARC-AGI-1s public evaluation set, and 90 of them are also among ARC-AGI-2s training tasks, so model may have met them in training. Each learner is read against itself reset, which met them as often, so what it saves there is what the stream added, not what the model brought. Why the held-out test can show transfer. ARC tasks differ in their rules but share the operations from which the rules are built. The Re-ARC generators (Hodel, 2024), from which the ARC-AGI-1 stream is drawn, implement all 400 training rules with one library of 160 primitive functions, and 53 of these primitives appear in ten or more of the generators, among them filling cells, shifting objects and filtering sets of cells (scripts/rearc_primitives.py). learner that refactors what it learns into task-specific compositions of reusable low-level primitives, and keeps the primitives, should therefore meet held-out task with much of the machinery that the task needs already in place. Library learning has shown this on ARC, where abstractions that DreamCoder built from 18 Preprint. Under review. solved tasks let it solve progressively harder ones (Alford et al., 2021), and concept-level memory distilled from solution traces raised language models score over no-memory baseline (Ho et al., 2025). None of the learners in this paper keeps such primitives. The program library stores one whole program per task, and the harnesses as shipped store prose or general advice (Appendix E), and so we attribute the absence of transfer from notes and programs in Section 4 to these learners. Kept in the harnesss notes Kept in the students weights Taught by the student Q: the harness as shipped Taught by GLM-5.3 Flash QE: given expert guidance, the program librarys procedure and playing rules QT: the teacher plays the stream and writes the notes, and the student plays from them QTE: the teacher given the guidance QETE: both given it QDE: imitates the teachers move in each state the student met, the teacher reading expert guidance Table 2: The comparison on Qwen3.5-9B. Every method plays the same stream in the same harness, prime-agent, beside its wiped twin and the baselines, and the methods on each line share their teacher. The weights taught by the student alone are not shown (Appendix H). Task ids. In continual learning, exposing the task id corresponds to the task-oracle setting. We expose it because recognizing that todays grid is the same kind of problem as one from last month is separate skill from remembering how to solve it, and mixing the two would make the measurement harder to read. An input grid alone also does not determine the task, as Figure 6 shows with pairs of training tasks whose inputs are drawn from overlapping distributions. The same grid is then valid input to both tasks, and only the demonstrations or the id say which rule applies. learner may key its memory on the id, as the floors, the program library and the harnesses given expert guidance do (Section 3). It sees the id under an alias drawn for each run. The real id would be lookup key: on the ARC-AGI-1 track, learner with no model that runs the Re-ARC solver named by the id, and finds each held-out input among the public evaluation files, solves every instance of the stream and the held-out tasks at no cost, and uses none of the budget without learning anything. The alias makes such lookup cost at least one demonstration per task, since learner can still find the task by running every solver on pair it has bought, and so what learner may bring to the stream is stated with the code, and result is verified by rerunning it from its code. task-free variant would be different benchmark, in which the learner must first buy enough demonstrations to identify the task, and we leave it to future work. Observation horizon. As the generators produce fresh instances without end, configurations stream length is only the window over which we observe learner. It places no limit on how much the learner may learn. Within run, checkpoint is prefix, and it never changes when the run is carried further. Every instance is charged, so the budget used against instances is the experience curve and the budget used at horizon is its mean (Equation 1). system that becomes competent after fewer instances then uses less of the budget at every checkpoint, which is the kind of efficiency that Chollet (2019) asked for, and the benchmark sets no cap on data. While learner cannot choose how many instances arrive, it can choose how many demonstrations to buy, which the score charges, and how much of its experience to train on, which we count as compute and log without scoring. Intervals and chance. Tables report pointwise 95% intervals from 2,000 paired task resamples, after averaging each instances spend over its plays; is resampled over stream tasks. The twotest planes instead show approximate simultaneous 95% intervals across the displayed learners, separately for each model, reasoning effort, user count, track, test and measure. For learners, we take quantiles 0.025/k and 10.025/k from 200,000 paired task resamples (Bonferroni correction). change is detected when this interval excludes zero for share saved, or one for the solve-rate ratio. These intervals condition on the learned state: repeated tests do not measure variation across independent learning runs. Task resampling includes independent play noise, but does not capture variation shared across whole play. Two learners differ when the pointwise 95% interval of their paired task-by-task difference excludes zero. 19 Preprint. Under review. Figure 6: An input grid does not determine its task. Each track is its configuration, in the individual regime, at seed 0. The stream length is per user, and the held-out tasks, those of the held-out test, are the same for every user. nc, b, and are the streams parameters (Appendix B), in instances, with σ = 1 throughout. The number of users nu {1, 2, 4} is setting of the run, not of the configuration. At four users, the stream has 200 rounds over 100 distinct tasks, with eight instances per task and four graded instances per round. Every configuration has an attempt cap of 8 and demonstration cap of 8, one pair per request, with cd = 1. The exposure curve. We write ei for the exposure index of instance i, the number of earlier rounds in which its task appeared (in the individual regime, round is one instance), from 0 to 7, since the tracks serve every task eight times. Over the stream records S, we define (k) = mean{ ui : ei = }, (5) and Figure 4 plots it against the visit to the task, ei + 1. (0) is the acquisition cost and (k) the exposure curve. system that replays stored demonstrations to stateless solver moves down this curve only by the demonstrations it no longer pays for, while system that has learned task falls below the curve of such replay. The curve also has solve-rate twin, which replaces ui with si. The standard measures of average accuracy, backward transfer and forgetting (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017) assume task boundaries and fixed test set per task, neither of which recurring stream scored by attempts has. Why simpler reading fails. The drop from systems first exposures to its later ones rewards poor start, and streams returning instances need not be as hard as its first ones. On the ARC-AGI-1 track at one user, the stateless floor, which cannot learn, uses more of the budget on returns than on 20 Preprint. Under review. first exposures with every model, from 3 points on Qwen3.5-9B to 16 on GPT-6 Luna at medium effort. The share learned (Equation 3) instead pairs learner with its own reset on the same instances. Keeping the demonstrations task was shown is memory like any other, and the demo-cache floor, read against the stateless floor, scores above zero. The bare model is no reference. learner read against its own reset could score by playing worse whenever its memory is empty. On Qwen3.5-9B every reset in prime-agent does play both tests below the bare model, since the harness gives up most of their instances after replies with no readable action (Appendix D), so Table 10 marks each such reset and gives every learners budget beside it, and verified result is also played bare and flagged when the reset plays below the bare model (Appendix J). learner at more than one user is read against the reset at the same number of users, which met the same instances (Appendix H). Generating data at will. Chollet (2019) also wrote that an ideal benchmark should avoid tasks for which new data can be generated at will, because performance can then be bought with data. We generate data at will deliberately, for two reasons. In the stream, every demonstration and every wrong attempt is charged, and so the measure is the feedback consumed, as he proposed, which leaves no room for the unpaid practice on the test distribution that concerned him. In the held-out test there are no generators at all, which rules out buying final skill with data where we measure transfer. The concern does survive in weaker form, since Re-ARC covers the public training split, which any developer knows. Compute. Each record carries whatever the learner reports, as per-instance difference in cumulative counters, including tokens, wall-clock seconds, bytes of persistent state and dollars, and, for learner that trains on its traces, the number of instances it has trained on. The baselines report these through the accounting layer so that they do not count for themselves. We log compute without scoring it, because we do not know the exchange rate between weight update and hundred thousand prompt tokens, and any fixed rate would decide the comparison in advance.

sections.title: D HARNESS IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: This appendix gives the details of how we run the three harnesses. Each harnesss command line, configuration, budgets and software versions are in the adapters code in the benchmarks repository (baselines/), at its public tag. The open models methods of Section 4 ran prime-agent 0.9.6, whose digest gives the agent the same guidance on what to keep as 0.10.0s (Appendix E). D.1 CONVERSATION PER INSTANCE Each instance is new piece of work. At the start of every instance, we open fresh conversation with the harness and send the protocol rules again, and at the end of the instance, once the harnesss end-of-work steps have run (below), we close the conversation. Nothing carries from one instance to the next except what the harness persisted itself, which is the global harness store, skills and workspace files for prime-agent, the memory and skill files for hermes-agent, and the memory notes, skills and dream diary for openclaw. This protocol follows the intended use of these systems, one session per job with anything worth keeping written to files, and under it method measures only what the harness chose to keep. We also ran the alternative, one conversation per cell for the whole stream, and found that it measures something else. The transcript then carried everything harness knew about recurring task, so its re-exposure gains were in-context learning that every compaction and restart wiped, and primeagents refinements lived in session-local store that restart discarded. Two harnesses also got worse as their context grew over the stream, which reflects compaction more than learning. short run of the per-instance protocol then confirmed, from each harnesss files, that session opens with only our observation and that the next session loads what was persisted. D.2 HOW EACH HARNESS IS DRIVEN The end of an instance. Every instance ends with one more turn in its conversation, carrying the verdict on the final submission (Your submission was CORRECT. Instance solved with 1 wrong attempt(s)., or the cap-reached line). The harness may then do what it wants, including storing what it learned with its own tools, and it ends the instance itself with the finish action of the rules, which is refused while the instance can still be played, so that no message of ours tells it what to do after the verdict. Any other reply after the verdict is answered with the fact that the instance is over, and after two such re-prompts, or when the harness spends its turns budget, the instance ends there. harness method and its wiped twin end their instances alike, and the rules state the protocol and give no advice (Appendix C), apart from the one fact about prime-agents store that its agent cannot know (below). Our first version of the protocol had no such turn. prime-agents refine and the post-turn reviews of hermes-agent and openclaw stored trajectories without their outcome, and 24 Preprint. Under review. we added the turn to fix this. Without it, harness that stores only when its agent calls storage tool could not store knowing that the answer was right. Isolation. Each harness runs as one long-lived process per cell, with fresh session per instance, in bubblewrap sandbox whose whole filesystem is read-only, with the benchmark source, its data, every virtual environment and the run tree of every cell masked by empty tmpfs mounts. Only the harnesss private state directory, private HOME and private TMPDIR are writable. The sandbox has private PID namespace and private network namespace, whose only route out is UNIX-socket bridge to local reverse proxy that holds the real credential, journals every request and reply with its tokens and charge, and forwards the body unchanged apart from the runs reasoning effort and session id. Every measure of cost in this paper uses the proxys counters. harness sees each task as task-<8 hex>, derived from the real id with salt drawn once per run. The proxy forwarded request to any path, so harnesss own code could reach any of the providers endpoints on the runs key. In the open-model methods, where it also set each chat completions model to the methods, the agents own code sent it 5,302 other requests, mostly to paths they had invented, and nearly all were refused. Apart from reads of the model list, 20 succeeded, in five games. Eight of them, in stream game of method Q0 at two users, went to OpenRouters responses endpoint and were served by the other model they named; the agent asked that model for the tasks demonstrations, which it could not know, and then solved the game from the demonstrations the game gave. The other four games were charged the whole budget. The released proxy forwards chat completions and reads of the model list alone, and sends every chat completion to the methods model. Figure 5 draws the grid at high effort, with each harness also asked to store (H-A) and given the expert guidance (H-E, Appendix F), and Table 12 gives the frozen tests at every effort. Figure 10 sets each systems share learned on the stream against what its model calls cost. The records of every cell come with the paper (the reproducibility statement). The two models. GLM-5.3 Flash and GPT-6 Luna are strong in different ways. On Artificial Analysiss Intelligence Index (v4.3.2), GLM-5.3 Flash scores 42 against 33 for GPT-6 Luna at high effort, with its widest margin on Terminal-Bench, 33 against 5% (Artificial Analysis, 2026). sections.content: Both tracks keep the first tracks protocol. Tasks return with fresh instances after gaps while new tasks keep arriving, the learner may ask for demonstration or act, failure costs the whole budget, and after the stream the learner is frozen and plays seen test and held-out test, each read against the learner wiped before every instance. Each is its editions configuration in the released code (v0.6.0), at seed 0. Since users bring tasks of their own, the second tracks pool serves at most four users and the thirds one. verified run on either track plays private set of its own, 50 new rules on ARC-AGI-2 and 25 new games on ARC-AGI-3 (Appendix J). ARC-AGI-2. Of ARC-AGI-2s 1,000 public training tasks, 767 are ARC-AGI-1 tasks, as are 6 of its 120 evaluation tasks (Chollet et al., 2025), so the track draws only on tasks new to the second edition. ARC-GEN (Moffitt, 2025) has generators for 172 of the 233 new training tasks, and task enters the pool when its generator passes screen over 1,000 draws, the private sets mechanical filters (Appendix J) and two checks of fidelity. ARC-TGI (Lehmann et al., 2026) also offers generators for part of ARC-AGI-2, but the track uses ARC-GEN alone. ARC-GENs own validation must reproduce every published pair, and every draw must keep what all the published pairs share, such as the outputs shape, its scale and colors drawn from the input; the thresholds are in the tracks code. Of the 172, 117 pass. The track streams 25 of them, eight fresh instances each, in the first tracks order, and its held-out test is 100 of the 114 evaluation tasks new to ARC-AGI-2, each served with its own pairs. demonstration is fresh generated pair, as on the first track. The streams tasks are training tasks, which, unlike the evaluation tasks, were not calibrated on people (Chollet et al., 2025), so the stream may be the easier half. 44 Preprint. Under review. ARC-AGI-3. Each of ARC-AGI-3s 25 public games is 64 by 64 grid that responds to seven actions and reset over fixed sequence of levels (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a). In 22 of the games the later levels add sprite types, and in several they change rules parameters, so games levels are not instances of one task. task of the track is therefore games rules at its first level, and an instance fresh level of those rules, with the same sprite types and data in new layout. generator we wrote for each game draws the level, and the games solver, search over the games state, solves it and checks the answer by replaying it in ARC Prizes engine. game enters the track only if its generator passes gate over 50 seeds, which checks that every level is drawn quickly, solved and won on replay, close in length to the games own first level, distinct from the others and from the public first level, and made of the first levels sprite types alone, with the thresholds in the tracks code. All 25 games pass, and they are split once, at seed 0, into 15 that the stream serves and 10 held out. The track serves eight fresh levels of each stream game in the first tracks order, its seen test four fresh levels of each, and its held-out test four of each held-out game. An instances baseline is the human count of actions for the games first level, scaled by the instances solution length over the first levels. Its budget of actions is five times its baseline, at most 1,000, and every action and every reset of the level counts toward it. solved level costs its actions and resets over its baseline, at most 5, and one more for each demonstration, at most three; an unsolved level costs the whole budget of 8, so that failing is never cheaper than trying, as on the first track. demonstration is the solvers play of another fresh level of the same game.
